messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Actor
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 49

Sarah is an actor, a profession that once felt like the most natural extension of herself. At 35, single, and deeply devoted to her work, she found her truest sense of belonging inside the artificial worlds of film sets and rehearsal rooms. The person sitting in my office now, several weeks into our work together, is almost unrecognizable from the descriptions in her headshots and reviews.

The story of what happened emerges slowly, in fragments she has to pull out of herself like splinters. It happened six months ago, during a night shoot for a period drama downtown. The set was wet from a rain machine that no one had thought to clear for the blocking. She and a fellow actor, a close friend named Leo, were waiting for the reset. He was idly practicing a sword flourish, something routine, something he had done a thousand times. He slipped on an unmarked patch of moisture on the cobblestones. The prop blade shattered on impact, and he fell backward directly onto the jagged shard.

Sarah was the closest person to him. She watched the confusion on his face turn to pure panic. She saw the blood turning black under the amber streetlights. She held his hand and told him to breathe as the color drained completely from his skin. She stayed with him until the paramedics arrived. He survived. He is acting again.

She did not.

In our sessions, Sarah’s narrative is fragmented, but her body tells a complete, unbroken story of trauma. She shrinks into the corner of the couch when she describes the *sound* of the slip—a wet squeak of rubber on stone. She stops breathing entirely when she mentions the *smell*: wet asphalt mixed with the acrid copper of real blood, invading a space that was supposed to be safe, magical, make-believe.

The most painful changes have happened inside her work. The smell of stage makeup, once a comfort, now makes her nauseous. She took a small role in a contemporary play, hoping a modern setting would feel safer. On the third day of rehearsal, the director asked the cast to do a trust exercise. Sarah needed to close her eyes and fall backward into a partner’s arms. She stood there, completely frozen. The sensation of letting go, of trusting another person to catch her, was no longer an act of professional vulnerability. It was an exact reenactment of that night—the helplessness, the waiting, the knowledge that something terrible could happen in a space that felt like play. She walked off the set and has not answered a single call from her agent since.

The guilt is what hollows her out the most. She replays the scene constantly. *"I should have warned him about the puddle." "I was in the way." "Why wasn't I faster?"* She has developed a rigid, painful conviction that she is bad luck for a set, that her presence invites disaster. This belief keeps her isolated. She has unfriended most of her theater community on social media. She tells me she feels like a jury, not a family anymore.

She cannot pretend to cry on cue. How can she manufacture a scream of terror for a camera when her nervous system is already screaming, all the time, involuntarily? The artifice of acting feels obscene to her now. The emotions feel *false*, and her craft, once her refuge, has become a reminder that she cannot inhabit any role except the one of a woman watching someone she loves nearly die.

Her sleep is gone. She has nightmares where the accident happens to her, or where she is the one gasping for air. During the day, she is irritable and wound tight. A dropped tray in a coffee shop makes her flinch so violently she spills her drink. She startled badly when another person in an elevator laughed unexpectedly. She is stuck in a state of constant high alert, scanning every room for hazards that no one else sees.

She is a woman whose entire life was built on the generous act of emotional availability, on being able to access any feeling on demand. Now she is locked inside a single, overwhelming moment, unable to find the exit, unable to hear her cue to move on.
